Stores and Shopping

Inside the grocery operation Amazon built to be pickier than you

From cherry taste tests to banana ripening rooms, here’s what happens before your Amazon groceries reach your door.

↓
By Alex Davies  ·  August 25, 2026

The first sign of trouble is how many cherries sprawled out on the table are missing their stems. Without them, the fruit breaks down faster. Standing in a field, Nick Moless can see too many stemless tops.

He picks up the palest cherry, cuts it open, and tastes it before squeezing a bit of its juice onto a refractometer. The handheld tool shines light through the liquid and measures how it bends to calculate the fruit’s sugar level. Low. He repeats the process with the darkest cherry, then really gets to work, spinning each fruit between his fingers, feeling for soft spots, holes, and dents, sorting them into rows of good and bad. The bad row grows long.

This box isn’t going to cut it.

A veteran of Whole Foods Market’s sourcing team, Moless leads Amazon’s produce and floral sourcing field team, and spends his days traveling from one supplier to the next. He’s one part of an operation backed by the same sourcing and quality standards that have served Whole Foods Market for years—one that involves field inspections, supplier relationships, temperature-controlled distribution, and multi-point quality checks. It’s a system built to address the commonplace, justifiable skepticism about online grocery: that whoever picks your produce won’t be as picky as you are.

“Just meeting the standard is kind of like a passing grade. We’re looking for the best of the best.”
Nick Moless · Produce and floral sourcing field team
Nick Moless, who leads Amazon’s produce and floral sourcing field team, gathers fresh fruits and veggies from suppliers across the U.S., from the cherry farms of the Pacific Northwest to the watermelon fields of the Southeast.

The cherry inspection is just one example of how Moless and his team ensure the best perishable products make it to customers, and it’s at the heart of Amazon’s grocery delivery operation. Getting fresh food to your door doesn’t start in a warehouse or an app. It starts in the field, before a product ever reaches a shelf or a screen. From there, inspectors like Moless decide what’s good enough to make the trip to one of Amazon’s Same-Day Delivery fulfillment centers, where all of that carefully sourced food is packed and out the door within hours. In dozens of cities, Amazon Now gets it there in 30 minutes or less.

The journey from farm to doorstep sounds simple enough, but behind it is a complex logistics puzzle. Amazon had to figure out how to get massive amounts of food—not just fruit and veggies, but milk, eggs, cheese, meat, seafood, bread, and more—from around the country and the world within a hop and a skip of its customers, without sacrificing quality along the way.

Doing so meant rethinking the fundamental idea of what the grocery store is. The result is a building that allows Amazon team members to pack customer orders not just quickly, but in a way that works for their recipients: bags organized by whether the food’s destined for the refrigerator or the cabinet; heaviest items at the bottom; no bag too full to neatly fold closed.

None of it works without the right product coming through the door, which is where the process begins. Items that carry Amazon’s Freshness Guarantee badge—available across Same-Day Delivery and Amazon Now—come with a promise: if it’s not up to standard, Amazon makes it right.
